findings.title: Purchase as attention exchange
findings.claim: The focus makes diversionary discourse something deliberately bought: it becomes an alternative stream that can carry attention and commitment away from God's path. In 4:44, misguidance itself is bought while others are wished astray from the way; in 9:9, God's signs are priced for little and the way is blocked. These wider exchanges let the focus's purchase read as a social transaction in guidance, not casual amusement.
findings.mechanism: The focus's Form VIII exchange verb takes diverting speech as its object, while the purpose clause names leading others away from a path. The independent scenes in 4:44 and 9:9 pair purchase with misguidance or obstruction of the way, so the focus's transaction gains a directional and social result.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees the purchase as competition for allegiance: the talk is acquired for what it does to the path and to other hearers.
findings.containment: No price, medium, or same actor group is specified in 31:6. The attention-market description is an inference from the focus's purpose clause and the wider exchange scenes; ordinary buying remains intact.

epistemic.reason: The focus branches are supplied at QAC occurrences and the cross-ayah Arabic is exact. The attention-allocation language comes from legacy readings and remains an interpretive inference.

findings.title: Misguidance by obscured landmarks
findings.claim: The focus can be heard as a route deprived of signs that make it trackable: the path, the waymark sense available in عِلْم, and the causative verb of misguidance meet in one navigational image. The wider closing scene in 31:34 makes the route image concrete by naming tomorrow's gain and even the land of death as things a person cannot know in advance; a path without its markers becomes practically unseen, not merely aimed at a wrong destination.
findings.mechanism: The focus path and waymark are the independent trigger for reading the disappearance branch on يُضِلَّ as loss of route visibility. The explicit unknown future and unknown place in 31:34 then extend that navigation problem beyond the focus.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees misdirection as loss of the signs by which a road can be followed, with an unknown horizon beyond it.
findings.containment: The QAC branch on يُضِلَّ remains a secondary image alongside ordinary causative misguidance. The 31:34 connection is interpretive context, not a claim that the same actors or event are described; the split-root road reading from د ر ي remains separate and attributed.

epistemic.reason: The focus branches and their exact QAC occurrences are supplied; the wider context is carried by legacy HFT traces whose word/root mapping remains attributed.

findings.title: The way taken as an object of mockery
findings.claim: The focus's taking-as verb makes its object something deliberately adopted for ridicule. In 45:9 the same clause follows an explicit mention of God's signs, and 5:57 describes religion itself being taken as mockery and play. Those wider echoes keep signs, the divine way, and religion live as possible referents of the feminine object; they do not settle the focus's open pronoun. The handle facet of taking adds an analogical image of seizing a guide as a prop for ridicule.
findings.mechanism: The focus pairs the act of taking with the result-category mockery. The exact repeated formula in 45:9 and the religious object in 5:57 independently meet that relation, while the handle facet is activated analogically by the taking-as construction and its mockery complement.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees mockery as an act of reclassification: a sign or way can be held up as a prop rather than received as direction.
findings.containment: The feminine pronoun in 31:6 remains structurally open. The handle image is analogical pressure from an available branch, not a literal translation of the Form VIII verb; the other ayat show live referents but do not prove the antecedent.

epistemic.reason: The focus QAC branches are supplied and the external wording is exact. The object identification and handle image remain contextual inferences; legacy and cross-run sources preserve more than one possible referent.

findings.title: Mockery returned as humiliation
findings.claim: The focus places deliberate mockery immediately before a punishment described as humiliating; the consequence returns the actor's contempt as loss of standing. The same mockery-and-humiliating-punishment wording appears in 45:9 after a reference to known signs, making the fit between offense and consequence a wider echo.
findings.mechanism: The taking-as and mockery words establish the outward act, while the punishment and its humiliating modifier give the consequence the same social register in reverse. The repeated formula in 45:9 provides the independent wider trigger.
findings.reader_payoff: The punishment's adjective becomes part of the answer to why the sentence names ridicule first: the outward lowering returns as the actor's own abasement.
findings.containment: This is a contextual reading of the juxtaposition, not a claim that every punishment mirrors its offense. The candidate's calm/dignity branch for مُهِينٌ is excluded: QAC supplies a Form IV active participle in the humiliation branch, while the positive calm sense has no independent carrier here. The focus word-analysis row also supplies a different root label, so the QAC-root carrier is qualified.

epistemic.reason: The focus branches and 45:9 wording support the mockery/punishment relation; the judgment that the consequence mirrors the act is interpretive, and the root analysis of the modifier is not uniform across supplied layers.

findings.title: A route socially replaced and later covered
findings.claim: The focus's bought diversion can be read as an early way a route is displaced socially: 31:21 shows people answering a call to follow revelation by following what they inherited from their fathers, and 31:32 ends a crisis-and-rescue sequence with knowing denial of signs. Together these later scenes make route replacement and its later covering newly visible alongside the focus's purchase and misdirection.
findings.mechanism: The focus carries an acquired diversion away from God's path. The response of inherited following in 31:21 supplies another route of refusal, while the post-rescue denial in 31:32 supplies a later form of covering; the focus phrase returns through diversion, path, and leading astray.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees a difference between the first displacement of direction and a later knowing refusal of signs, without assuming that the verses describe one actor.
findings.containment: The retrospective source is legacy-unbound, and the relation between these separated scenes is an inference. 31:21 and 31:32 may be parallel cases rather than stages in one continuous biography.

epistemic.reason: The wider ayah texts and HFT roles are supplied, but the sequence linking them to the focus is a qualified retrospective synthesis.

findings.title: Limits on claiming and refusing direction
findings.claim: The focus treats directing others without knowledge as a fault. In 31:15, a person may refuse a coercive command that itself lacks knowledge while still keeping good company and following an evidenced path; 31:34 then marks future gain and the place of death as knowledge no person owns. Together these contexts make the boundary of misdirection clearer: principled refusal is not the same act as directing others without knowledge, and future direction cannot be claimed as possession.
findings.mechanism: The focus's knowledge and path words return in 31:15, where refusal and following are separated, and in 31:34, where future outcomes exceed human knowledge. These distinct scenes meet at the question of who may claim authority to direct.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can distinguish unsupported direction from an evidence-based refusal and can see why claims about the future need a boundary.
findings.containment: This combines two legacy HFT readings that may operate independently. No claim is made that the focus's buyer appears in either context or that 31:34 directly rebukes the focus.

epistemic.reason: The candidate summary is not independently anchored, but its two stated contexts are supplied in exact HFT/connection evidence; the synthesis remains an inference.

findings.title: Speech judged by where it leads
findings.claim: The focus condemns discourse used to occupy and lead people away; Luqman's speech in 31:13 is a warning that aims to reorient its hearer. The wider example makes the point about the focus's hadith word: speech is not condemned as a medium in itself; what matters here is whether it occupies a hearer away from the path or recalls the hearer toward it.
findings.mechanism: The focus's word for speech meets its diversion word, while 31:13 supplies articulated speech and admonition as a separate function. Their contact shifts the focus from a class of entertaining speech to a contrast in what speech does to attention and direction.
findings.reader_payoff: A reader can keep the focus's warning intact while seeing why speech itself can also guide.
findings.containment: The HFT record attributes the context roots and word indices, and its own note allows genre or speaker authority as another explanation for the contrast. The claim is functional and does not identify the same speaker or hearer.

findings.title: Refusal under pressure can preserve the path
findings.claim: The focus's `without knowledge` and path language can be read beside 31:15, where a coercive, knowledge-free command is refused while companionship is maintained and another path is followed. The wider scene changes the boundary of the focus's misguidance charge: a refusal of unsupported pressure can preserve direction rather than abandon it.
findings.mechanism: The focus's knowledge and traversable-path branches meet the 31:15 sequence of pressure, refusal, good companionship, and selective following. This separates movement away from a demand from movement away from the path.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see that not every refusal or departure from a social demand is misguidance.

findings.title: Discourse without three checks
findings.claim: The focus warns about bought talk used to lead people away without knowledge. In 31:20, a structurally parallel disputant is described as arguing about God without knowledge, guidance, or an illuminating book. The added checks turn the focus's missing knowledge into a wider picture of persuasive argument that lacks both direction and inspectable textual light.
findings.mechanism: The repeated human and knowledge-free frame links the focus's hadith to the context's argument verb; the additional absence of guidance and an illuminating book supplies two independent checks that the focus does not name in the same phrase.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees the speech as capable of becoming a whole argumentative system whose persuasiveness exceeds its grounding.
findings.containment: The HFT reader explicitly allows 31:20 to be a neighboring case of the same broader failure rather than the cause of 31:6. Context branch roots and word indices remain attributed.

epistemic.reason: The Arabic of both ayat is supplied and the focus contact is repeated syntax; the HFT's contextual roots and causal relation remain attributed.

findings.title: A holding that can bear weight
findings.claim: The focus presents a bought diversion and an adopted act of mockery. In 31:22, submission to God is pictured as grasping a firm handhold and trusting what is reliable. The juxtaposition lets the focus's purchase and taking-as act be measured against an attachment that can actually be held with confidence.
findings.mechanism: The focus's acquisition and adoption acts meet the context's verbs of holding and trusting. The handhold image supplies an independent criterion of dependability and changes the question from which content is chosen to what kind of attachment can bear weight.
findings.reader_payoff: A reader sees the actor's chosen attachment alongside a contrasting image of secure reliance.
findings.containment: The HFT itself allows that the hand imagery may be rhetorical rather than causal; the focus's feminine object remains open, and the context's word/root assignments are attributed.

epistemic.reason: 31:22's exact Arabic supplies the handhold and trust image; the specific HFT roots and coordinates remain attributed.

findings.title: A small present return and a hidden cost
findings.claim: The focus's purchase of enjoyable diversion ends in punishment. In 31:24, brief enjoyment is followed by compulsion into punishment; in 31:33, the warning not to be deceived by worldly life and the deceiver names the risk of trusting the near benefit. Together these scenes make the purchased diversion look attractive because a small return is visible now while its cost is not.
findings.mechanism: The focus's purchase, play, and punishment meet 31:24's temporary benefit and compulsion, then 31:33's explicit warning about deception. The later scenes supply the temporal gap and deceptive salience that the focus leaves compressed.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see how immediate enjoyment and delayed consequence belong to one decision horizon.
findings.containment: The HFT source says the two warnings may stand independently; no claim is made that 31:24 or 31:33 describes the same buyer or intentionally hides a future cost.

epistemic.reason: The HFT trace supplies exact context coordinates and Arabic, but target morphology and same-actor continuity are not established.

findings.title: Two supplies of discourse
findings.claim: The focus makes diverting talk something bought and consumed as a product. In 31:27, pens and replenishing ink are imagined on a scale that still cannot exhaust God's words. The contact changes a simple contrast between idle and true speech into a contrast between a finite, acquired discourse stream and meaningful address whose supply exceeds material writing.
findings.mechanism: Purchase and speech in the focus meet the context's writing implements, replenishing ink, non-exhaustion, and intelligible words. Those material supplies make the focus's marketable discourse comparable to one kind of supply, while the denial of exhaustion marks the other as beyond scarcity.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees not only what each discourse says but how each is supplied: one can be bought and renewed as product, while the other is pictured as inexhaustible.
findings.containment: The HFT inference itself warns that 31:27 may concern divine magnitude rather than media competition. The focus does not say its buyer intends to replace the words of God, and the 31:27 writing image is an analogy rather than a literal communications industry.

epistemic.reason: The HFT gives exact focus/context coordinates and roles, but every 31:27 root assignment is attributed because target morphology is not supplied.

findings.title: Crisis strips the surface layer
findings.claim: The focus's diversion can act like an occupying layer over acknowledged dependence. In 31:32, overwhelming danger is followed by undivided invocation, rescue, and then knowing denial of signs; crisis briefly strips the competing layer, while safety allows refusal to return.
findings.mechanism: The focus's occupation branch meets 31:32's covering danger, turbulent wave, purification, sincere religion, rescue, and post-rescue denial. The before-and-after sequence makes crisis function as a stress test on the diversion's hold.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees distraction as recoverable rather than permanent: danger can remove it for a moment, and safety can allow it to be rebuilt.
findings.containment: Fear alone could explain the changed behavior; the reading does not prove that a media-like diversion was literally removed or that the same actors occur in 31:6 and 31:32.

epistemic.reason: The exact context Arabic and HFT trace are supplied, but all non-focus roots/roles remain attributed and the stress-test relation is inferential.

findings.title: Purchasable direction and unowned futures
findings.claim: The focus joins purchase, path, and absence of knowledge. In 31:34, each soul lacks knowledge of tomorrow's gain and the place where it will die. This wider limit lets the focus's bought direction look like confidence packaged as possession in a domain where future return and endpoint cannot be owned by a human buyer.
findings.mechanism: The focus's knowledge noun anchors its deficit, the path supplies practical direction, and the purchase verb supplies acquisition. The future gain and death-place in 31:34 meet those carriers and show what no person can possess in advance.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees the offense as more than an information gap: it can be a confident sale of a future direction that no buyer can guarantee.
findings.containment: The HFT reader allows 31:34 to remain a general epistemic boundary. The purchase-as-possession reading is an inference, and the context does not identify the same buyer.

epistemic.reason: The exact HFT coordinates and Arabic are supplied; context roots are attributed and the commerce-to-future relation remains interpretive.

findings.title: Purchased novelty as a feed process
findings.claim: The focus's purchase verb and new-talk branch can make the diversion appear as a stream of fresh units fed into an attention process. The grain-feed branch on لَهْو is a concrete but form-distant analogy; 31:27's pen and replenishing ink give the process a wider supply echo.
findings.mechanism: Buying supplies deliberate intake, حديث can carry new occurrence, and the mill-feed branch supplies an image of material entering a process. The later ink feeding a pen meets that process image and makes diversion look continually produced rather than a single finished message.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can picture diversion as a process that keeps receiving new material, not only a one-off item someone buys.
findings.containment: The HFT's own containment is controlling: the mill-feed branch is surprising and form-distant, valid here only as a process analogy joining purchased لهو, renewed talk, and the later ink-supply echo. It is not a lexical translation.

epistemic.reason: This reading depends on a legacy-unbound HFT trace and an explicitly form-distant analogy; its links are retained as exploratory.

epistemic.reason: The connection rows supply exact target Arabic but no target morphology or trust label; the semantic contact is grounded in the supplied wording and remains contextual.
